passage: Raghav, you've known me, Ishita, since school, so you know I don't shout at people. You want to know why I apologised to a total stranger on the 8:10 local? It was May, the compartment was packed, and I had someone's elbow in my ribs and sweat running down my back. A woman's bag kept knocking my arm and I just snapped: 'Can you keep your stuff to yourself?' Loudly. Everyone looked. She said sorry, very quietly, and three stations later I felt awful. Now I notice when the heat starts making my chest tight. I drink water before I board, stand near the door if I can, and tell myself, 'It's the crush, not her.' Most bumps I just let go. And that day I found her at the exit and said sorry back.

qa.q: What did Ishita say to the woman on the train?
qa.a: 'Can you keep your stuff to yourself?'

qa.q: How did Ishita feel three stations later?
qa.a: Ishita felt awful and guilty for snapping at someone who was squashed in the same crowd.

qa.q: What could help Ishita on the next hot, packed ride?
qa.a: Drinking water before boarding, standing near the door when possible and remembering 'It's the crush, not her' help Ishita let small bumps pass.

qa.q: What was it like for the woman when Ishita snapped at her?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed with everyone looking, since her bag was bumping only because of the crush; she answered with a quiet sorry.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a hot, packed train whose short fuse leads to snapping at a stranger, and who learns to recognise the heat and crowding and let small provocations pass.

passage: I'm Vijay. I've ridden the college bus with Yogesh for two years, and he's usually the one cracking jokes. Last Thursday the bus sat in traffic for forty minutes, windows jammed, bodies pressed right up to the steps. A boy behind us kept kicking Yogesh's heel. Yogesh turned, face red and wet, and said, 'Kick me once more and see.' The boy went pale. I pushed my water bottle into Yogesh's hand. He drank half of it, shut his eyes, and after a while muttered, 'Sorry, yaar, I'm just cooked.' When we got off, he bought the kid a lime soda at the stall. I can't say what was going on in his head, only that the heat seemed to have wound him tight.

qa.q: How long was the bus stuck in traffic?
qa.a: The bus sat in traffic for forty minutes.

qa.q: What do Yogesh's red, wet face and sharp warning suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed angry and overheated; the heat and crush had shortened his temper, so a small kick felt like a big provocation.

qa.q: Which choice helped cool things down, and why?
qa.a: Vijay handing over water and Yogesh shutting his eyes gave a pause; once calmer, Yogesh apologised and made up with the boy.

qa.q: What was the moment like for the boy who kicked Yogesh's heel?
qa.a: He was probably shocked and scared, going pale at the warning, and may have been kicking only because he was squashed too.

grounding: Shows, through a friend's eyes, a young adult whose temper shortens on a hot, crowded bus, and how a pause and water help a small provocation pass.

passage: Zainab, you know me, na? Deepak the peacemaker. Last Tuesday I squeezed into the 8:10 fast at Dadar. June, no breeze, bodies pressed so tight I could feel an elbow in my ribs and sweat running down my back. Then an uncle stepped on my foot and I just exploded: 'Are you blind?' The whole compartment turned to look. He mumbled sorry, and I felt terrible for the rest of the ride. Since then I've been trying something. When the heat hits, I tell myself, 'This is the train talking, not me.' I breathe out slowly and sip water at each station. Yesterday someone's bag hit my face, and I just let it go.

qa.q: What did Deepak shout at the man who stepped on his foot?
qa.a: 'Are you blind?'

qa.q: How did Deepak feel after snapping?
qa.a: He felt terrible and embarrassed, since he sees himself as a peacemaker and the whole compartment turned to look.

qa.q: What is Deepak's new approach, and why does it help?
qa.a: He reminds himself the heat and crowd are feeding the anger, breathes out slowly and sips water, so small bumps can pass.

qa.q: What might the man who stepped on Deepak's foot have felt?
qa.a: He was probably startled and embarrassed, since in a packed train it was most likely an accident.

grounding: A young man in a hot, packed train snaps at a stranger and learns to recognise the crowd's effect and let things pass.

passage:
Monday: The city bus was packed and airless. Uday, sweating through his shirt, got shoved at the door and elbowed the man back so hard they nearly came to blows. His friend Vijay pulled him off a stop early. 'Bro, what was that?' Uday had no answer.
Thursday: Same bus, same heat. Uday felt the tightness climbing his neck. He remembered Vijay's question, moved near a window, drank from his bottle and counted his breaths out.
The next Monday: A woman's bag swung into his arm. Uday felt the flash of anger, then heard himself say, 'It's fine, it's crowded,' and meant it.

qa.q: What did Uday do on Thursday when the tightness climbed his neck?
qa.a: He moved near a window, drank from his bottle and counted his breaths out.

qa.q: How did Uday feel after nearly fighting on the first Monday?
qa.a: He felt shaken and confused; he had no answer for why he had elbowed the man so hard.

qa.q: What changed between the two Mondays?
qa.a: Uday learned to notice the heat and crowding building in his body and to cool down before reacting, so he could let a bump pass.

qa.q: What might Vijay have felt pulling Uday off the bus?
qa.a: Vijay was probably alarmed and worried that his friend was about to get into a real fight.

grounding: Over a week a young man on a crowded bus learns that recognising the heat's effect helps him let small provocations pass.

passage: Akash, you came home fuming about the crowded metro, so let your Vasudha Dida tell you something. When I was in college, I took the Howrah bus every day. In May the tin roof burned like a tawa and we were packed like mustard seeds. One afternoon a lady's umbrella poked my neck and I screamed at her in front of everyone. Then I saw she was old, carrying a sick child. I cried all the way home from shame. My friend Ranu told me, 'In that bus the heat does the fighting, not you.' After that I would feel the anger rise, wipe my face, sip from my steel bottle and let it pass. Most pokes are only accidents, beta.

qa.q: What poked young Vasudha's neck on the bus?
qa.a: A lady's umbrella.

qa.q: How did young Vasudha feel after screaming at the lady?
qa.a: She felt deeply ashamed and cried all the way home once she saw the lady was old and carrying a sick child.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vasudha's bus story?
qa.a: Ranu's remark that the heat does the fighting; after that Vasudha noticed the anger rising, cooled down and let small pokes pass.

qa.q: How might the old lady with the sick child have felt when Vasudha screamed?
qa.a: She likely felt startled and hurt, already struggling in the heat with a sick child.

grounding: A grandmother recalls snapping on a packed, hot college bus and learning to let small provocations pass.

passage: The 8:12 local was twenty minutes late, and by the time it crawled into Dadar, Hemant was pressed between a wet shoulder and someone's lunch bag, sweat running down his back. It was his first week at the internship and he could not be late. When a man's elbow jabbed his ribs for the third time, Hemant snapped, "Can't you stand properly?" The man glared, and for a second both of them puffed up. Then Hemant caught his own reflection in the window, red and scowling, and remembered Sarika's text that morning: "Heatwave today. Don't pick fights on the train." He let out a breath. "Sorry, bhai. It's the heat." The man shrugged. "Everyone's cooking in here." At Lower Parel Hemant stepped off, bought water and gulped half of it before walking to the office.

qa.q: How late was the 8:12 local?
qa.a: Twenty minutes late.

qa.q: Why did Hemant snap at the man?
qa.a: He was hot, squeezed and anxious about being late in his first week, so his temper was short.

qa.q: What helped Hemant let the moment pass?
qa.a: Seeing his own scowl, remembering Sarika's text about the heat, breathing out and apologising, then drinking water.

qa.q: How might the man have felt after Hemant's apology?
qa.a: He probably felt less defensive, even friendly, agreeing that everyone was cooking in there.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a hot, packed train snapping at a stranger, then recognising the heat and crowding and letting the moment pass.
